statement: Different two-digit numbers are chosen. What is the smallest number of them that must be chosen to be certain that three of the chosen numbers have the same digit sum?

choices.misconception: I worked out how many are needed for two numbers with the same digit sum, not three.
I found 34 numbers with no three sharing a digit sum and gave that, forgetting one more is needed to force it.
I noticed that digit sum 1 has only one two-digit number, 10, but missed that digit sum 18 also has only one, 99.
I used 18 boxes with two numbers in each and added one, ignoring that some digit sums have fewer than two numbers.

hints: List the possible digit sums and how many numbers have each.
Use the digit sums as boxes. To avoid three in a box, take at most two numbers from each box, but some boxes do not even hold two numbers. Count the largest set with no three alike, then add one.
Digit sums run from 1 to 18. Sum 1 has only 10 and sum 18 has only 99; every other sum has at least two numbers.

solutions.reliable: The digit sums of two-digit numbers run from 1 (only 10) to 18 (only 99), and every sum from 2 to 17 has at least two numbers, for example 11 and 20 for sum 2 and 89 and 98 for sum 17. To avoid three with the same sum, take at most two numbers per sum: at most 1 + 16 × 2 + 1 = 34 numbers, and 34 is achievable. So 34 numbers might not be enough, but any 35 force three with the same digit sum. The answer is 35. The transferable idea: in a pigeonhole argument, the worst case fills each box as far as the box allows, and small boxes hold less.

whyOnTest: Pigeonhole questions need the true worst case: some boxes are too small to hold their share, and missing that gives the near-miss answers.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
